title: Multisystem Uveitis: The Diagnostic Puzzle
summary: An 18-year-old female presenting with recurrent red eye, cough, arthralgia, oral ulcers, and skin nodules suggests a complex systemic inflammatory syndrome. This clinical picture primarily points toward Behçet’s Disease or Sarcoidosis, requiring a rigorous multidisciplinary workup to prevent irreversible ocular and systemic morbidity.

sections.title: Clinical Case Synthesis & Overview
sections.content: The constellation of recurrent uveitis, aphthous stomatitis (oral ulcers), polyarthritis, and erythema nodosum (skin nodules) in a young adult is a classic presentation for Behçet’s Disease (BD). However, the presence of a cough necessitates the exclusion of Sarcoidosis, Tuberculosis, and Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (GPA). In ophthalmology, these systemic diseases manifest as sight-threatening panuveitis or retinal vasculitis.

sections.title: International Criteria for Behçet's (ICBD)
content: Oral Aphthosis (Mandatory in older criteria): 2 points
Genital Aphthosis: 2 points
Ocular Lesions (Uveitis/Vasculitis): 2 points
Skin Lesions (Pseudofolliculitis/Nodules): 1 point
Neurological Manifestations: 1 point
Vascular Manifestations: 1 point
Positive Pathergy Test: 1 point (optional)
Diagnosis: Score ≥ 4 points is diagnostic.

sections.title: Pathophysiology: The Neutrophilic Blitz
sections.content: Behçet's is an autoinflammatory vasculitis. It is characterized by hyperactive neutrophils and Th1/Th17 mediated response. Unlike Sarcoidosis, which is granulomatous, Behçet's features a sterile, neutrophilic infiltration leading to tissue necrosis and vascular occlusion.

sections.title: Red Flags: Ocular Emergencies
content: Sudden, painless vision loss (Central Retinal Artery Occlusion)
Thunderclap headache (Dural Sinus Thrombosis)
Severe hemoptysis (Pulmonary Artery Aneurysm Rupture)
Numbness/Weakness (Neuro-Behçet's)
Hypopyon with severe pain (Endophthalmitis Mimic)

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup: Step-by-Step
content: Step 1: Baseline Labs - CBC (Leukocytosis), ESR/CRP (Elevated), ANA/RF (Exclude SLE/RA).
Step 2: Pathergy Test - Prick forearm with 20G needle; read at 48h for sterile pustule.
Step 3: Imaging - Chest X-Ray or HRCT Chest (Look for Hilar Adenopathy for Sarcoid).
Step 4: Ocular Imaging - Fluorescein Angiography (FA) to detect 'fern-like' leakage and capillary non-perfusion.
Step 5: Ancillary Ocular - OCT for Macular Edema; ICG for choroidal involvement.
Step 6: Multidisciplinary Consult - Rheumatology and Pulmonology referral.

rows: Anti-TNF alpha agents are highly effective for BD

sections.title: Surgical Considerations
content: Cataract Surgery: Delay until 3 months of complete quiescence.
Pars Plana Vitrectomy (PPV): Indicated for non-clearing vitreous hemorrhage or tractional RD.
Glaucoma: Often secondary to steroids or synechiae; may require tube shunts.
Intravitreal Implants: Ozurdex (Dexamethasone) can be used but risk of IOP spike.

content.explanation: B: Blood clots (Vasculitis); E: Erythema nodosum; H: Hypopyon (Shifting); C: CNS involvement; E: Eye (Panuveitis); T: Triad (Oral, Genital, Eye); S: Skin pathergy.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls & Landmark Evidence
content: Pearl: The Behçet's hypopyon is 'cold' and moves with head position, unlike the 'sticky' hypopyon of HLA-B27.
Evidence: The VISUAL I & II trials established Adalimumab as a steroid-sparing agent for non-infectious uveitis.
Pearl: Always check for genital ulcers; patients are often embarrassed to report them.
Observation: Retinal veins in Behçet's often show 'perivascular cuffing' and 'sheathing' early in the disease.
